questions: Does 'closest vowel from the right side' mean the vowel nearest to the end of the word that is between two consonants, or the first vowel encountered when scanning from right to left that is between two consonants?
Are 'y' and 'Y' considered vowels or consonants?
Should the function be case-sensitive in checking vowels and consonants, or only in returning the vowel?
What constitutes a consonant? Is it any non-vowel letter, or are there special cases?
If a vowel is between two consonants but one of those consonants is at the word boundary, does it count?
For words with multiple vowels between consonants, do we return all matching vowels or just one?
What should be returned if the word has no vowels or is empty?
Does 'between two consonants' require the consonants to be immediately adjacent to the vowel?
answers: It is the first vowel encountered when scanning from right to left that is between two consonants.
They are considered consonants because only 'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u' and their uppercase forms are vowels.
It is case-sensitive in both checking and returning, as the vowel set includes uppercase and lowercase.
A consonant is any English letter that is not a vowel (i.e., not in the set of 'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u' and their uppercase).
No, vowels at the beginning or ending do not count, so boundaries are excluded.
Return just the first one found when scanning from right to left.
Return an empty string, as also done for words with length less than 3.
Yes, the vowel must have a consonant immediately before and after it.
